title: CS 4400 — Computer Systems
summary: 6 assignments and 4 labs spanning x86 simulation, reverse engineering, cache optimization, shell implementation, malloc design, and concurrent network programming for CS 4400

data.text: A deep dive into computer systems for CS 4400 at the University of Utah across 6 assignments and several labs (Spring 2026), progressing from machine-level instruction execution through reverse engineering, performance optimization, process control and signals, virtual memory and dynamic allocation, to concurrent network programming. The course followed the CS:APP (Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective) textbook and built up systems expertise layer by layer — from writing an x86-like processor simulator that decodes instructions via bit masking and executes them on a register file, to defusing a binary bomb without source code, to squeezing cache performance out of image-processing kernels with loop blocking and sliding-window algorithms, to building a full Unix shell with job control and pipe support, to implementing a custom malloc with segregated free lists and boundary-tag coalescing, to writing a multi-threaded HTTP server with semaphore synchronization and federated friend discovery. Labs reinforced each topic with focused exercises in buffer overflow attacks, process trees with fork/execve, inter-process communication through pipes, and mmap-based memory allocation. All code was written in C.

items.content: Instruction decoding via bit masking: parsed 4-byte instructions by extracting fields with bitwise operations — opcode from bits 27–31, first register from bits 22–26, second register from bits 17–21, and a 16-bit signed immediate from bits 0–15, using right shifts and masks to isolate each field

Register file and execution engine: implemented a processor with 17 named registers (including %rsp and %rbp), a 1024-byte stack, and a program counter that indexes 4-byte instructions, executing ~20 opcodes covering arithmetic (addl, subl, imull), data movement (movl with register-indirect addressing via memcpy), and stack operations (pushl/popl)

Flags and conditional execution: computed condition flags after cmpl — carry flag via unsigned overflow check, zero flag via equality, sign flag from bit 31, and overflow flag by detecting sign-bit disagreement between operands and result — then used them to drive conditional jumps (je, jl, jle, jg, jge) with the correct signed/unsigned semantics

Control flow: implemented call (push return address, jump to target), ret (pop return address, jump back), and unconditional/conditional jumps, enabling the simulator to run recursive and branching programs on its custom ISA

Reverse engineering without source: defused a multi-phase binary bomb using only GDB and objdump disassembly — no source code was provided, so each phase required reading raw x86-64 assembly, identifying the expected input format, and determining the correct passphrase or numeric sequence to avoid detonation

x86-64 disassembly analysis: traced register usage, memory accesses, and control flow through optimized machine code, recognizing compiler-generated patterns for loops, conditionals, string comparisons, linked-list traversals, and recursive calls

GDB debugging: set breakpoints at key comparison instructions, inspected register and memory state mid-execution, and used watchpoints and single-stepping to reverse-engineer the logic of each bomb phase without triggering the explode function

Complex rotation+grayscale kernel: optimized an image kernel that simultaneously rotates and converts to grayscale using 8×8 loop blocking (tiling) to keep working data in cache, pointer arithmetic instead of array indexing to eliminate repeated multiply-offset calculations, 4× loop unrolling within each tile, and __attribute__((always_inline)) on helper functions to remove call overhead

Motion blur with sliding window: replaced the naive 3×3 convolution (9 reads per pixel) with a sliding-window algorithm that computes the initial column sums once, then subtracts the departing column and adds the arriving column as the window moves right — reducing redundant memory accesses from O(9n) to O(3n) for interior pixels

Edge-case handling: implemented separate code paths for interior pixels (divide by 9), edge pixels (divide by 6), and corner pixels (divide by 3), using bit-shift division (>> 2 and >> 1) where the divisor was a power of 2 to avoid expensive integer division, and adjusting the sliding-window logic for the narrower windows at image boundaries

Cache-aware data access: structured all loop traversals to access memory in row-major order matching C's array layout, maximizing spatial locality so that each cache line fetched is fully utilized before eviction — the single biggest performance lever for both kernels

Full shell implementation: built a Unix shell supporting foreground and background job execution, built-in commands (quit, jobs, bg, fg), and pipe chains (cmd1 | cmd2) — parsing command lines, forking child processes, and managing a job list that tracks PID, job ID, and run state

Pipe support: implemented single-pipe command chains by creating a pipe(fd), forking two children where the first dup2s its stdout to the pipe's write end and the second dup2s its stdin from the pipe's read end, then closing unused file descriptors in each child to prevent deadlock on EOF

Signal handling: installed handlers for SIGCHLD (reap terminated or stopped children via waitpid(-1, &status, WNOHANG | WUNTRACED)), SIGINT (forward Ctrl-C to the foreground process group), and SIGTSTP (forward Ctrl-Z to suspend the foreground job), using sigprocmask with sigfillset to block all signals during critical job-list updates

Race condition prevention: blocked SIGCHLD before fork() and unblocked after the child was added to the job list, ensuring the handler cannot reap a child before the parent has registered it — the classic signal-masking pattern for avoiding TOCTOU races between fork and job-list insertion

Foreground waiting with sigsuspend: used sigsuspend(&empty) in a loop checking a global fg_pid flag rather than busy-waiting or calling waitpid directly — atomically unmasking signals and sleeping so that SIGCHLD delivery is the only wakeup, avoiding both race conditions and wasted CPU cycles

Terminal control: transferred terminal ownership to the foreground process group with tcsetpgrp(0, gid) so that child processes receive keyboard signals, then restored terminal control to the shell after the foreground job completes — each child calls setpgid(0, 0) to form its own process group

Stack smashing exploit: exploited a stack buffer overflow in a program with a vals_to_sum[4] array and no bounds checking on the user-supplied num_vals count — by writing past the array's bounds, overwrote the saved return address on the stack to redirect execution to a nevercalled() function

Stack layout analysis: mapped out the stack frame to understand the offset between the buffer and the return address, calculating exactly how many extra values to write and what value to inject so that ret pops the attacker-chosen address instead of the legitimate caller

data.text: Lab 7 — Process Trees with fork & execve

items.content: Process tree construction: used fork() to create a target tree of processes matching a required pstree diagram, then called execve from the parent to run pstree -p on the first child's PID to verify the structure — coordinating with sleep() to ensure all forks complete before the snapshot

execve mechanics: set up the argument array ({"/usr/bin/pstree", "-p", pid, NULL}) and environment ({NULL}) for execve, converting the child PID to a string with sprintf — reinforcing that execve replaces the current process image entirely and never returns on success

Pipe-based IPC: built a microbash that forks a writer and a reader process — the writer sends 5 random bytes to stdout with random 1–3 second delays, and the reader continuously reads one byte at a time from stdin, printing each byte's arrival timestamp to demonstrate that read() blocks until data is available

Understanding blocking I/O: the lab demonstrated how pipes naturally synchronize producer and consumer — the reader's read(0, &readbyte, 1) call blocks when the pipe is empty and returns 0 (EOF) only when all write ends of the pipe are closed, making the pipe the synchronization primitive itself rather than requiring explicit locks

Segregated free lists: organized free blocks into 10 size classes (16 B to 4096 B+), each with its own explicit doubly-linked free list — mm_malloc searches the appropriate size class first, falling back to larger classes, so small allocations don't have to scan past large free blocks

Boundary-tag coalescing: each block carries a header and footer (PACK(size, alloc)) so that mm_free can check both the next block's header and the previous block's footer in O(1) to determine whether to merge — implementing all four coalescing cases (neither neighbor free, previous free, next free, both free) to combat external fragmentation

Block splitting: when the best-fit free block is larger than needed, set_allocated splits it into an allocated portion and a new free remainder (if the remainder is at least the minimum block size), keeping internal fragmentation low while maintaining the free-list invariant

Page-level memory management: extended the heap using mem_map/mem_unmap with an exponential page-growth strategy (doubling the page size on each extension, capped at 64 KB) — and returned fully-freed pages to the OS when page_count > 1, balancing allocation speed against memory footprint

16-byte alignment: all returned pointers are aligned to 16-byte boundaries as required by the x86-64 ABI, with block headers and footers sized so that the payload starts at the correct alignment regardless of the block's position within a page

Custom heap with mmap: allocated a 4096-byte region via mmap(NULL, 4096, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANON, -1, 0) and implemented a bump allocator that advances a pointer through the region — a minimal allocator that trades the inability to reuse freed memory for extreme simplicity

Linked-list data structure: built a doubly-linked list of strings on the custom heap, with each node storing three pointers (data, prev, next) accessed through macros (DATA(l), PREV(l), NEXT(l)) — supporting add (with deduplication), remove (by relinking neighbors), and display operations

Thread-per-connection architecture: spawned a new POSIX thread for each incoming HTTP connection with pthread_create and immediately detached it with pthread_detach, so each client is served concurrently while the main thread loops back to accept() — the simplest concurrent server model that avoids the serialization of a single-threaded design

Semaphore synchronization: protected the shared user dictionary with a binary semaphore (sem_init(&sem, 0, 1)) using P(&sem)/V(&sem) wrappers to ensure mutual exclusion — every read or write to the shared data structure is bracketed by lock/unlock to prevent data races between concurrent handler threads

REST API endpoints: implemented four HTTP endpoints — /friends?user= (list a user's friends), /befriend?user=&friend= (add a mutual friendship), /unfriend?user=&friend= (remove a mutual friendship), and /introduce?user=&friend=&host=&port= (federated friend discovery) — parsing query parameters from the HTTP request line and returning plain-text responses

Federated friend discovery: the /introduce endpoint turns the server into an HTTP client — it opens a connection to a remote server with Open_clientfd, sends a GET request for the remote user's friend list, parses the newline-delimited response, and adds each remote friend as a mutual friend of the local user, demonstrating server-to-server communication

Signal-masking race conditions in tsh: the shell's job list could be corrupted if SIGCHLD arrived between fork() and addjob() — solved by blocking SIGCHLD with sigprocmask before forking, adding the job while signals are blocked, then unblocking afterward so the handler never sees a child that isn't in the list yet

Pipe file-descriptor leaks: forgetting to close unused pipe ends in the shell caused readers to hang waiting for EOF — systematically closed the write end in the reading child, the read end in the writing child, and both ends in the parent after forking, following the rule that every pipe() creates two FDs that must be closed in every process that doesn't use them

Coalescing edge cases in malloc: boundary-tag coalescing required careful handling when a free block sits at the start or end of a page — an off-by-one in the footer pointer calculation would read into an adjacent page's header, producing phantom merges or segfaults; solved by adding sentinel checks at page boundaries before attempting to read neighbor tags

Sliding-window correctness in motion blur: the sliding-window optimization produced incorrect blur values at image edges where the 3×3 kernel extends past the boundary — fixed by computing separate sums for edge and corner regions with adjusted divisors (9 for interior, 6 for edges, 3 for corners) rather than clamping or padding

Flag computation in the x86 simulator: getting all four condition flags correct for cmpl required treating the same operands as both signed and unsigned simultaneously — carry flag checks the unsigned subtraction for borrow, while overflow flag checks whether two same-sign operands produced an opposite-sign result, and mixing up the two produced subtly wrong conditional-jump behavior that only surfaced on specific test inputs

x86 machine-level programming: instruction encoding and decoding, register files, condition flags (CF/ZF/SF/OF), conditional execution, call/return mechanics, and reverse engineering compiled binaries with GDB and objdump

Performance optimization: cache-aware programming with loop blocking/tiling, spatial and temporal locality, loop unrolling, strength reduction (replacing division with bit shifts), sliding-window algorithms to eliminate redundant memory accesses, and function inlining

Process control and signals: fork/exec/wait process lifecycle, process groups and terminal control, Unix signal handling (SIGCHLD, SIGINT, SIGTSTP), signal masking with sigprocmask for race-condition prevention, sigsuspend for safe blocking, and async-signal-safe programming

Inter-process communication: Unix pipes (pipe/dup2), file descriptor management and the importance of closing unused ends, blocking vs. non-blocking I/O, and EOF semantics in producer-consumer pipelines

Dynamic memory allocation: segregated free lists, explicit doubly-linked free-list management, boundary-tag coalescing (header/footer metadata), block splitting, page-level memory mapping with mmap/munmap, alignment requirements, and the fragmentation-vs-utilization tradeoff
Security: buffer overflow attacks, stack smashing, return-address overwriting, and understanding how unchecked array bounds become exploitable vulnerabilities

Network programming: socket API (accept/connect/read/write), HTTP request/response parsing, building both server and client sides within a single program, and query-parameter routing for REST-style endpoints
Concurrency: POSIX threads (pthread_create/pthread_detach), shared-state synchronization with semaphores, mutual exclusion for thread-safe data structures, and the thread-per-connection server model

Systems programming in C: pointer arithmetic, bitwise operations for instruction decoding and flag computation, void* casting, macro-driven data structures, memcpy/memset for raw memory manipulation, and low-level system calls throughout every assignment
